av_event.line_text: Mm. Somebody's whole life, maybe, that roof.
av_event.what: At the right edge of the frame a T-shirt slips off the clothes airer behind Tomasz and drops out of view to the floor, with a faint soft thump on the mic; Tomasz doesn't turn round.

text:
B: Hello, mate. Colin, down in Worthing. Can you hear me alright?
A: Yes. Hello, Colin. Tomasz, in Exeter.
B: Tomasz. Have I said that right?
A: Yes, perfect. Better than most people.
B: I did a bit of Spanish at evening class, so I'm very careful with names now. I saw your Dartmoor map in the picture. I put down you looked like a teacher.
A: Erm, no. Student. Archaeology, second year. And I work on a packing line, in a factory, nights and weekends.
B: Archaeology! Oh, I'm jealous now. I left school at sixteen, did my apprenticeship, never looked back. Except I did, later on. In lockdown I did an online course on the history of architecture, and I loved it more than anything I'd done in years. I thought, why didn't I do this at twenty?
A: I'm doing it at thirty-seven, so. Maybe it's never too late. Or maybe it is, I'll tell you in two years.
B: Ha. What got you into it, then?
A: Erm, it's a long answer. In Lublin there's the old town and a castle on the hill, and my grandmother used to take me round and tell me who was killed where, which for a child is very exciting. I started history at university there, then I left, came here for factory work, and I thought, okay, that's finished. Fifteen years. Then Hannah, my wife, she sort of pushed me to do the Access course at the college. And now I'm here.
B: That's not a long answer, that's a good answer.
A: Thank you. You were a builder?
B: Joiner. Kitchens, staircases, doors. My favourite was old sash windows, though, restoring them. You open one up and you can see how some bloke did it in eighteen-ninety, and he did it better than me, usually.
A: That's archaeology too, a bit. Reading a building.
B: Is it? I'll put it on my CV.
A: Really. In old buildings they look at how the timber was cut, the tool marks, and it helps to date it.
B: Tool marks, yeah. I did a job on a church roof once, years ago, and you could see the adze marks on the beams, every one a bit different. Somebody's whole week, that beam.
A: Mm. Somebody's whole life, maybe, that roof.
B: That's it. That's why I want to see Japan, the old wooden temples. Before the knees go.
A: Hannah wants Crete. Knossos. I want it too, but she wants the beach as well.
B: Oh, you can do both. We did Granada, the Alhambra. I've never seen anything like it. All that carved plaster, it's like lace.
A: When were you there?
B: Ooh, er, let me think. Twenty-twelve? Thirteen? Not the most organised with dates. We missed the train back to Málaga, I remember that.
A: I don't plan either. I book everything last minute. Hannah gets very angry.
B: Maureen too. Thirty-odd years she's been angry, and I've still not learnt.
A: Good. So there's no hope for me. That's relaxing.
B: Ha, none at all, mate. What are you reading at the minute, apart from all the uni stuff?
A: Lem, again. Polish science fiction. And a book about old field boundaries, which sounds boring, but it's not.
B: I'd read that. I've got three library books on the go and I'll finish one, if I'm lucky.
A: I have four. I think the library is worried about me.
B: They'll send someone round. What's the field boundary one, is it —
